title: Chapter 26 – The Longest Night
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Feng]

The tea is boiling, and nobody has lit a fire.

Lin Feng watches the kettle on the guardroom table with the dull fascination of a boy who has not slept in thirty hours. A slip of orange paper lies under it, no bigger than a thumb, curled at the edges and glowing from within like an ember in a snowdrift. A Fire Starter, half a copper in the market. Kai crushed it into the kettle's belly twenty minutes ago and has been guarding it since, like a hen.

"It's done," says Kai.

"It's been done."

"I wanted to be sure."

"You always want to be sure." Feng takes the kettle by the handle. His left leg gives a long, cold twinge as he stands, the old twinge, the one that began in the rain on the day a man in a feather cloak laid two fingers on his thigh and said nothing at all. Third Aunt says the Blood Qi is dead. Third Aunt also says it takes a year to leave the marrow. He ignores it, as he has ignored it for eight months, and pours.

There are eight of them in the guardroom beside the north gate. The runners. It is the name Grandfather gave them in the spring, when the first of the Zhao patrols began to ride the road: eight young Lins who can climb a wall in the dark, throw a talisman at forty paces and run a message across the hill in the time it takes to boil rice. Feng is the oldest, at fifteen, and the best of them at nearly everything. He is also, since the council, the one the others look at when they want to know whether they should be afraid.

He has been practicing his face for a week.

"The north road is quiet," says Lin Qiao, who is fourteen and a wind-slip fanatic, with a talisman clipped in each sleeve and one more in her hair. "Dong's on the wall. Ping's at the west postern. The east pins are lit; I checked them twice."

"Three times," mutters Dong, from the doorway, where he is leaning on his shield.

"Three times, then." Qiao takes her cup. "And nothing's moving. Not a lantern, not a dog."

"That's what worries me," says Kai.

It is what worries all of them. Feng looks at the eight faces over the rims of eight cups, tired and scrubbed and very young, and thinks of his father's saying about the quiet before a storm. He thinks that his father, wherever he is on the wall tonight, would not say it aloud.

"Drink," he says. "Then we do the rounds."

* * *

Uncle Wenyuan's workroom is warm and smells of cedar and ink.

It is two hours before midnight, and the lamp on the long table has burned down to a smudge. His uncle sits at the head of it with his sleeves pushed back and his left hand lying open on the wood. It does not shake. Feng has been looking at it for three weeks, ever since the night of the third pill, and has not yet got used to it.

"Sit," says Wenyuan. "All of you. Quickly."

They sit. Eight of them, shoulder to shoulder, on a bench built for four. On the table before them is a long row of slips, each in its own square of white cloth, laid out in rows like a merchant's stall. Yellow and gray and orange. Ink so fresh the smell still hangs in the air.

"There are forty-two," says Wenyuan. "Five for each of you, and two for Feng, who will need them more. You will sign for them with your thumb and you will account for every one afterward, spent or not. They cost half a month of my evenings." He glances up. "I do not mind. I mind waste."

He touches the first row. "Refined Iron-Skin. Mortal. Press to the chest and say your own name. It will turn a blade, a stick, a fall from a roof. It will not turn a Qi Refining Eighth. Count on three breaths and not four."

The second. "Greater Cloudstep. Two paces in any direction, no faster than thought, no slower than a stumble. Good for a door. Bad for a long fall."

The third, in bright orange. "Flame-Burst. Pepper-ink, Jian's receipt, twice the sting. Throw at the face. Not the chest. The face. If you hit the chest you've wasted it."

"We know, Uncle," says Kai.

"Then you will know it better in the morning." Wenyuan lifts a fourth slip, thin and gray. "Ancient Featherfall, for the wall. Beast-Calming, for the dogs. And one Royal Blood-Staunching apiece. If a friend is cut, you say your friend's name, not your own. I want that clear." He looks along the row. "I want every one of you to come back in the morning with all your slips used or none of them. I do not want you to come back with the wrong number of friends."

Nobody laughs. It is not a joke.

He hands them out one by one. When Feng's turn comes, he takes the slips from his uncle's right hand and finds them warm. Two extra: a pale blue Fever-Cooling, and a plain white one that he does not recognize.

"What is this?"

"Sound Mirage." Wenyuan's mouth quirks. "I drew it this afternoon. It throws your voice thirty paces. You may use it when you need to be somewhere else."

Feng turns it over. The ink is perfect, a single unbroken line of black, and the character at the center is the one his uncle uses for home.

"Uncle," he says, and stops.

"Yes?"

He had meant to say a good many things. That he was sorry for the winter, when he had called his uncle's hands useless. That he had been wrong. That he would stand in front of anyone who came through that gate. He finds that none of it will come out, and says instead, "The sword."

"Ah." Wenyuan's eyes go to the practice sword slung at Feng's hip, a plain steel blade in a plain scabbard. "Jian told me nothing about it."

"He didn't tell me anything either."

"No. He has been very efficient at that lately." Wenyuan lays his hand on the table beside the slips. "You have a stubborn mind, nephew. You are going to carry it into a fight in the morning. Try to remember that the person you are fighting is also stubborn, and also afraid, and also, probably, a friend of somebody." He pauses. "And then kill him if you have to. But remember."

"Yes, Uncle."

"When this is over," says Wenyuan, "I am going to teach you the second form of the Lin Blade. You will like it. It is much more ill-mannered than the first."

Feng laughs. It surprises him. It comes out of him like a hiccup, and Kai laughs, and Qiao, and for a moment all eight of them are only boys and girls on a bench in a lamp-lit room, and nobody in the room is afraid.

* * *

The granary cellar lies under the oldest barn on the hill, down eleven steps of packed earth, behind a door that Hu fitted with a bar of spirit iron and a Door-Sealing slip.

Feng goes down at eleven with a basket of rice buns. It is not an errand. It is a thing he has been telling himself he must do, in the manner of a boy who has been told to check the pantry for mice. At the bottom, in the dim yellow light of a Light Orb slip hung from a nail, he finds nine children and three women sitting on sacks of barley, under the quiet eye of Aunt Meirong.

She is Wenhai's wife and Lin Hu's mother. She is thirty-six, and she has not spoken to anyone above a whisper since the council. When she sees Feng, she rises from her sack, folds her hands in front of her, and bows.

"Don't," says Feng, appalled.

"I would like to, Nephew." Her voice is very quiet. "It is the only thing I have to give."

He sets down the basket. Lin Yue, who has been asleep with her head in a sack of oats, wakes, looks at him, and says, quite clearly, "Is Jian coming?"

"Jian's busy."

"He's always busy." She takes a bun. "He said he'd tell me a story."

"Then you'll hold him to it."

"I will." She bites it, solemnly. In the corner, a boy of eleven with a long nose and his father's habit of biting his lip is sitting on an upturned crate with his back to the wall. He has not touched a bun. He looks at Feng with eyes that are old and dry and very frightened.

Feng crosses the cellar and crouches in front of him.

"Hu."

"Is my father alive?"

Feng has been asked a great many hard questions in his life. Most of them have been about sword forms. He thinks of his uncle's advice about the sorrows of fighting people who are also somebody's friend, and he thinks that Wenyuan, who was always better at this than he was, would find something wise to say.

"I don't know," he says. "Aunt Su says they're holding him in a room in the east wing. That's all I know."

"They will kill him."

"Maybe."

"He deserves it."

"Yes," says Feng, because it would be a lie to say otherwise. "And I'm sorry."

The boy looks at him for a long time. Then his chin goes up, very slightly, and Feng sees what has been going on in the lamp-lit corner of the cellar all night: that a child who has watched his father be named a traitor in front of thirty-one adults is sitting very straight, because he has decided that whatever the Lins say about his father, no one will be able to say it about him.

"When it starts," says Lin Hu, "will you come and tell me?"

"I'll send someone."

"Not someone. You."

Feng considers. "If I can."

"That's an honest answer," says Lin Hu, and takes a bun, and eats it, very slowly, all the way to the end.

* * *

He tests the sword alone, in the stable yard, at midnight.

It is a thing he has been putting off. The blade came back from the forge three weeks ago, apparently unchanged, with a small, smug smile from his youngest cousin and a conversation Feng has been replaying ever since. The book? The book. It had struck him at the time as a lie so thin that it was almost a joke. Now, in the dark, with the horses breathing and the lantern hissing, he draws the blade from its sheath and looks at it.

It is steel. It is the same steel. He knows every nick on it. But the light moves along the edge strangely, as along the lip of a bowl of water, and when he lays a thumb flat against the spine he feels something he has never felt before in a weapon: a sort of alertness.

A spare pin lies on the anvil in the corner, one of Hu's, a good one-inch bar of black iron, dull from a month in the rack. He sets it across two stones. He raises the practice sword.

Crescent Edge, he thinks, and a thin curve of pale Qi runs along the blade, the sort of thing every Lin boy learns by twelve.

He cuts.

There is no sound. That is what he will remember: no ring, no spark, no shriek of metal. The blade passes through the bar like a knife through a pear, and the two halves lie on the stones with their ends bright as mirrors, and the blade is whole.

He stands for a long time looking at it.

Hardness fifty-eight, Jian's voice says in his head, which is absurd, because Jian did not say it. Jian never says anything. But Feng has watched his cousin for seventeen years, from the day the baby in the cradle looked up at him with a pair of grave black eyes that were far too old and he thought, with the fierce condescension of a six-year-old, this one is going to be trouble. And in nine years he has learned one thing about Lin Jian above all the others: that the quiet ones do not stay quiet. They wait until the last moment, and then they hand you the sword.

He sheathes it. His hand is shaking, slightly, and he looks at it with irritation.

"It's a good blade," says a voice from the dark.

Feng's own hand is on the hilt before he knows he has moved. Su Qinghe steps out of the shadow by the well. She is wearing her working short robe and has the Tidal Spear on her back, and in the lantern light her face is composed and weary. She must have been standing there a good while.

"Aunt."

"It is a very good blade." She looks at the two halves of the bar. "Do not tell anyone how good."

"I wasn't going to."

"No. You were going to tell yourself that you were not afraid of what it means." She comes closer. "Feng. I need to ask you something, and I need you to hear it as an order."

"Yes."

"Today, when the fighting starts, you will be at the gate. That is your place. Hu will be there, and Wenyuan, and Mao, and the cousins. It will be loud. It will feel like the whole world." She tucks a strand of hair behind her ear. "But there is a door behind the main hall, in the stone hut, that opens on a stair. Whoever stands in front of that door is standing in front of the Patriarch. And in front of Jian."

"Jian went down?"

"Grandfather took him an hour ago. I do not know why. I only know that it is a thing he has decided, and that when he decides a thing, it is done." Her gaze is steady. "If the line breaks, Feng, if the wall falls and the gate goes and every one of us is down, you will not die at the gate. You will go to that door. You will stand in front of it. You will not let anyone through who is not Lin."

He swallows. "Aunt, I'm not afraid of Zhao Qian."

"You should be." Her voice is not unkind. "He is better than you. Older, with more Qi and a better saber, and no scruples at all. But he is also afraid of one thing in the world, and it is not a thing I can name." She almost smiles. "He is afraid that he will be beaten by someone he thought was beneath him. It has kept him alive for twenty years. Do you understand?"

"No."

"Good. Neither do I. Go and eat something."

She walks away across the yard, a small straight figure under a sky full of stars. He stays where he is for a long moment, with the sword at his hip and the lamp spitting in the cold, thinking about a boy he has known all his life, and a door.

* * *

At the second hour past midnight, the alarm flares.

He is on the east wall when it happens, with Kai and Qiao, eating cold rice from a bowl he is not tasting. A brief red flash from the ridge above the pins. A sound like a cat in a bag, thin and high and furious, and a yellow spark that darts across the dark like a firefly.

"That's Jian's," says Qiao.

"I know."

"He set a Boundary Alarm on the ridge. Yesterday. I saw him do it."

"I know, Qiao." Feng puts down the bowl. "Stay here. Kai, with me. Qiao, wake Dong and tell him to hold the postern. If you see a light, ring the bell. Not the little one."

They go over the wall by the east stair, quickly, in the dark, with their cloaks pulled close and the Wind-Veil slips folded in their palms. It is three hundred paces to the ridge. He covers them in a trot, listening to the night. The pins are silent underfoot, which is correct, because the wire has not been tripped. The alarm has simply seen something that is not a step.

He sees it at fifty paces.

A man, bent double in the grass, working with his hands. Gray-green cloak. A short sword on his hip. He is crouched over a flat stone beside the wall, and in the dim starlight Feng can see the faint gleam of a yellow slip. He is pressing it into the mortar of the retaining wall, carefully, like a man planting a seed.

Beacon. Feng knows the shape of it even from here. A Royal Emergency Beacon, a Yellow Grade talisman. You set it in a place where it will not be found, and the moment its surroundings change, a pulse in the ground, a flare of light, a shift in the vein, it burns and sends a signal anyone with a Seeing Mirror can read from five miles away.

Somebody wants to know the instant something happens on this hill.

"Kai," he breathes. "Left. Wide. When I move, throw."

Kai nods and is gone.

Feng takes eleven steps forward, in the long grass, with his weight low. At the twelfth, the man's head comes up.

He is young, maybe twenty, with a thin face and a Zhao ridge-and-sun badge stitched on the shoulder. He sees Feng, and his hand goes to his belt. He pulls a slip, gray, with a thread of ink running diagonally across it, and slaps it against his own chest.

Iron-Skin. A good one.

Feng does not wait. "Kai!"

The Flame-Burst goes off at the man's left flank with a bark like a dropped door. Orange light blooms. He lurches, one arm up, and Feng comes in with the ash spear, low and fast, and the crescent of Qi along the blade lifts the man's guard.

The scout is a Qi Gatherer, perhaps the fifth stage. Feng is faster. But the man is also trained, and does not lose his head. He cuts, a short flat arc that skims the spear's haft and nicks Feng's forearm, and kicks the spear aside, and before Feng can reset his feet, he has pulled a second slip from his sleeve.

Thunderclap.

Not in my face, you bastard. Feng throws himself sideways. The slip goes off in a single crack like a bolt of lightning striking a dry branch, and the air around them shatters. A wall of white noise slams into his left ear, and his vision turns to snow.

He is on his knees. He cannot hear. The man is above him, short sword raised.

Falling Leaf, he thinks, and has no breath to cast it, and does not need to. The spear shaft comes up from the ground in his hands with all the weight of the dawn drills he has run with his youngest cousin, a short vicious rising strike that takes the scout under the chin. The man's head snaps back. His sword falls. And then Kai is on him with a cord, and it is over.

Feng sits in the dust with his ears ringing and his forearm bleeding and watches the scout being tied.

"You're hurt," says Kai.

"It's a scratch."

"It's deep."

"Say my name," says Feng, "and use the slip."

Kai produces the Blood-Staunching, and presses it to the wound, and says "Lin Feng" in a shaky voice. The blood slows. The pain does not.

The scout, tied and propped against the wall, opens his eyes. He looks at them. And then, with great slowness, and a faint, thin smile that makes Feng's skin crawl, he says, "You found the first."

"There's only the one," says Kai.

"There were three." The man's voice is slurred and amused. "The young master said you'd find one. Perhaps two. The cousin is clever. But the third..." He coughs. "The third was set a long time ago. By someone who knew the hill."

Feng's stomach goes cold.

"Where?" he says.

The scout shuts his eyes and does not answer.

* * *

They find the second beacon in a quarter of an hour, under a root on the north side of the same ridge, and burn it.

They do not find the third.

They search until dawn. Feng goes along the wall with a dark lantern, one stone at a time, the Spirit-Sight slip glowing faintly against his palm, while Kai and Qiao take the postern and the stable yard. They turn over every mossy crack in the retaining wall. They comb the grass inside the yard, the well, the kitchen garden. He kneels in the dust and puts his hand on the cold bricks of the stone hut itself, and feels nothing at all.

Someone who knew the hill.

He knows who. He does not say it aloud.

The sky begins to gray at the eastern edge, a thin line, like a blade held to the light. A cock crows in the yard. Somewhere behind him a door opens, the low door of the stone hut at the back of the compound, and a small figure steps out into the half light.

It is Lin Jian. He is alone. He has his father's gray cloak on over his tunic and a bronze disk the size of a coin clutched in his left hand. He stands on the threshold with the door open behind him and the dark stairway yawning at his back, and he does not look at the yard, or the wall, or Feng. He looks at the sky, at the line of light along the ridge, with the expression of someone doing a sum.

Then, very carefully, he pulls the door shut. Behind him, a bar drops into place with a sound like the end of a sentence.

Feng takes a step toward him. "Radish."

The boy turns. For a moment he seems to see nothing. And then his eyes focus, and he looks at his cousin's bandaged arm, the dirt on his face, the sword at his hip. "You found the other two," he says.

"You knew about them?"

"I guessed." Lin Jian's gaze goes to the stone hut's roof. "Did you find the third?"

"No."

"I thought not." He says it quietly, without surprise. "Feng. When the ring lights, do not go near the hut. Whatever you hear."

"What's in there?"

"My grandfather," says Lin Jian. "And the rest of the morning." He pockets the bronze disk. It has a pine crest on one face. "Go and sleep an hour, if you can. You look terrible."

He walks off across the yard toward the kitchen, a small, straight, grave figure, and does not look back.

And then the hut begins to glow.

It starts at the foundation, a thin blue light, creeping up between the stones like water rising in a cup. It fills the seams, climbs the walls, lights the roof tiles from underneath. The twelve pins of the great ring come alight one by one around the hut, each a small cold star set in the earth, and Feng, standing in the middle of the yard with his bandaged arm and his useless lantern, has the sudden and overwhelming sense of standing at the edge of something very large, very old and very slowly waking.

Behind him, in the trees, every cicada stops.

The silence comes down like a lid.

"Feng." It is Kai, hoarse. "Feng, look."

He turns.

Across the valley, to the east, on the dark shoulder of the ridge above Red Ridge, a single thread of smoke is climbing into the new morning. It is thin and white and perfectly straight, rising from a place where there was no fire a moment ago. As Feng watches, it bends, once, in the wind, as a signal bends when it has been read.

It is answered. Far off, a second thread climbs from the next hill. Then a third.

The third beacon has burned.

He stands there with his sword and his talismans and his bleeding arm and thirty-one hours without sleep. The sun clears the ridge. The smoke goes on climbing.

"Ring the bell," says Lin Feng. "The big one."
